blocks.en: "What is man that You are mindful of him...? You have made him a little lower than the angels." — Psalm 8:4–5 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué es el hombre, para que tengas de él memoria...? Le has hecho poco menor que los ángeles." — Salmo 8:4–5 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 1 — What Preaching the Doctrine of Man Must Do
blocks.es_reference: Día 1 — Lo que debe lograr predicar la doctrina del hombre

blocks.en: Having preached God, we now preach the creature made to know Him. The doctrine of man holds a paradox the preacher must keep whole: man is at once crowned with glory and fallen into ruin — made in God’s image, yet a sinner. The aim is not to flatter the hearer (“you are wonderful”) nor to crush him (“you are worthless”), but to tell him the truth that prepares him for grace: you are greater than you think and worse than you fear, and only Christ answers both.
blocks.es_reference: Habiendo predicado a Dios, ahora predicamos a la criatura hecha para conocerlo. La doctrina del hombre sostiene una paradoja que el predicador debe mantener entera: el hombre es a la vez coronado de gloria y caído en ruina — hecho a imagen de Dios, y sin embargo pecador. El objetivo no es adular al oyente (“eres maravilloso”) ni aplastarlo (“eres un don nadie”), sino decirle la verdad que lo prepara para la gracia: eres más grande de lo que piensas y peor de lo que temes, y solo Cristo responde a ambas cosas.

blocks.en: "What is man that You are mindful of him...? You have made him a little lower than the angels, and You have crowned him with glory and honor." — Psalm 8:4–5 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué es el hombre, para que tengas de él memoria...? Le has hecho poco menor que los ángeles, y lo coronaste de gloria y de honra." — Salmo 8:4–5 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 2 — The Doctrinal Backbone (lean; see Systematic Theology Units 5–6)
blocks.es_reference: Día 2 — El fundamento doctrinal (breve; vea Teología Sistemática, Unidades 5–6)

blocks.en: Man is made in the image of God (Gen. 1:26–27) — the ground of all human dignity, the reason every person matters. Man fell into sin. “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23); the image is defaced but not erased. Depravity means sin reaches every part of us — not that we are as bad as we could be, but that no part is untouched, so we cannot save ourselves. Yet man retains worth and potential, for he is still God’s image-bearer and the object of God’s redeeming love (John 3:16). The whole doctrine answers the hearer’s deepest question about himself: what am I, and what is wrong with me?
blocks.es_reference: El hombre es hecho a imagen de Dios (Gén. 1:26–27) — el fundamento de toda dignidad humana, la razón de que cada persona importe. El hombre cayó en pecado. “Todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios” (Ro. 3:23); la imagen queda desfigurada, pero no borrada. La depravación significa que el pecado alcanza cada parte de nosotros — no que seamos tan malos como podríamos ser, sino que ninguna parte queda intacta, de modo que no podemos salvarnos a nosotros mismos. Y sin embargo el hombre conserva valor y potencial, pues sigue siendo portador de la imagen de Dios y objeto del amor redentor de Dios (Jn. 3:16). Toda la doctrina responde a la pregunta más honda del oyente sobre sí mismo: ¿qué soy, y qué hay de malo en mí?

blocks.en: Day 3 — The Homiletical Move
blocks.es_reference: Día 3 — El movimiento homilético

blocks.en: Subject: man. Interrogative: “What is the truth about man?” Keyword: truths (a plural noun). Four points, each on its own text, and arranged to move from height to depth to hope:
blocks.es_reference: Tema: el hombre. Interrogativo: “¿Cuál es la verdad sobre el hombre?” Palabra clave: verdades (un sustantivo plural). Cuatro puntos, cada uno sobre su propio texto, ordenados para moverse de la altura a la profundidad a la esperanza:

blocks.en: Point (keyword: truths)Anchor text
blocks.es_reference: Punto (palabra clave: verdades)Texto base

blocks.en: 1. Man is made in God’s image (his glory)Genesis 1:26–27
blocks.es_reference: 1. El hombre es hecho a imagen de Dios (su gloria)Génesis 1:26–27

blocks.en: 2. Man has fallen into sin (his ruin)Romans 3:23
blocks.es_reference: 2. El hombre ha caído en pecado (su ruina)Romanos 3:23

blocks.en: 3. Man cannot save himself (his need)Ephesians 2:1, 8–9
blocks.es_reference: 3. El hombre no puede salvarse a sí mismo (su necesidad)Efesios 2:1, 8–9

blocks.en: 4. Man is loved and redeemable (his hope)John 3:16
blocks.es_reference: 4. El hombre es amado y redimible (su esperanza)Juan 3:16

blocks.en: The order is the sermon’s power: glory, ruin, need, hope. The hearer is lifted, humbled, emptied, and then pointed to Christ — an arc that bends naturally toward the invitation.
blocks.es_reference: El orden es la fuerza del sermón: gloria, ruina, necesidad, esperanza. El oyente es levantado, humillado, vaciado, y luego señalado a Cristo — un arco que se inclina naturalmente hacia la invitación.

blocks.en: Before developing a point as a sermon, let each truth be understood for what it is. They move in an arc — glory, ruin, need, hope — and the hearer must feel each turn.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de desarrollar un punto como sermón, entienda cada verdad por lo que es. Se mueven en un arco — gloria, ruina, necesidad, esperanza — y el oyente debe sentir cada giro.

blocks.en: 1. Man is made in God’s image — his glory (Genesis 1:26–27). Alone among the creatures, man was made in the image of God: able to know Him, to reason, to choose, to love, to create, to be held to account. And because we bear that image, every one of us has worth — worth that no circumstance can cancel. The homeless man has it. The stranger has it. The immigrant has it. We do not lose our worth when life goes against us, for it was never grounded in our success or our standing; it is grounded in the image stamped upon us. In that sense all people are God’s children, made by Him and loved by Him, and it remains His desire to bring every one of them home. There is, to be sure, a different sonship for the believer — the adoption that comes by faith in Christ — but God’s love reaches all, and the worth of every soul stands secure. So tell the hearer who counts himself nothing the truth older than his shame: you bear the image of the living God.
blocks.es_reference: 1. El hombre es hecho a imagen de Dios — su gloria (Génesis 1:26–27). Solo entre las criaturas, el hombre fue hecho a imagen de Dios: capaz de conocerle, de razonar, de escoger, de amar, de crear, de ser responsable. Y porque llevamos esa imagen, cada uno de nosotros tiene valor — un valor que ninguna circunstancia puede cancelar. El indigente lo tiene. El extranjero lo tiene. El inmigrante lo tiene. No perdemos nuestro valor cuando la vida se nos pone en contra, pues nunca estuvo fundado en nuestro éxito ni en nuestra posición; está fundado en la imagen grabada en nosotros. En ese sentido todas las personas son hijos de Dios, hechas por Él y amadas por Él, y sigue siendo su deseo traer a cada una a casa. Hay, por cierto, una filiación distinta para el creyente — la adopción que viene por la fe en Cristo — pero el amor de Dios alcanza a todos, y el valor de cada alma queda seguro. Así que dile al oyente que se cuenta por nada la verdad más antigua que su vergüenza: tú llevas la imagen del Dios vivo.

blocks.en: 2. Man has fallen into sin — his ruin (Romans 3:23). But the image is defaced. From the first man we inherited a sinful nature, and “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” The ruin is not partial; it reaches mind, will, and affection alike — what we call total depravity: not that a man is as wicked as he could be, but that no part of him is left untouched. So deep does it run that even his noblest efforts are stained — his very best, offered to a holy God, is the filthy rag. He is worse than he fears.
blocks.es_reference: 2. El hombre ha caído en pecado — su ruina (Romanos 3:23). Pero la imagen está desfigurada. Del primer hombre heredamos una naturaleza pecaminosa, y “todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios.” La ruina no es parcial; alcanza la mente, la voluntad y los afectos por igual — lo que llamamos depravación total: no que el hombre sea tan malvado como podría ser, sino que ninguna parte de él queda intacta. Tan hondo corre que aun sus esfuerzos más nobles están manchados — lo mejor de él, ofrecido a un Dios santo, es el trapo inmundo. Es peor de lo que teme.

blocks.en: 3. Man cannot save himself — his need (Ephesians 2:1, 8–9). “And you He made alive, who were dead in trespasses and sins.” Mark the word: not sick, but dead. A sick man may take medicine and mend; a dead man can do nothing for himself at all. This is why salvation must be “by grace... through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works.” Here the sermon empties the hearer of his last secret hope in himself — the résumé, the good intentions, the comparison with worse men — so that, having nothing, he will at last look outside himself for a Savior. He is more helpless than he admits, and the admission is the door.
blocks.es_reference: 3. El hombre no puede salvarse a sí mismo — su necesidad (Efesios 2:1, 8–9). “Y Él os dio vida a vosotros, cuando estabais muertos en vuestros delitos y pecados.” Note la palabra: no enfermo, sino muerto. Un enfermo puede tomar medicina y sanar; un muerto no puede hacer nada por sí mismo. Por eso la salvación debe ser “por gracia... por la fe; y esto no de vosotros, pues es don de Dios; no por obras.” Aquí el sermón vacía al oyente de su última esperanza secreta en sí mismo — el currículo, las buenas intenciones, la comparación con hombres peores — para que, no teniendo nada, mire al fin fuera de sí mismo por un Salvador. Es más impotente de lo que admite, y la admisión es la puerta.

blocks.en: 4. Man is loved and redeemable — his hope (John 3:16). And here the whole arc turns. The God who stamped the image and watched it fall did not walk away from the ruin — “God so loved the world.” But this is the point left for you to develop in Day 4, so we say no more of it here than this, and hand you the joy of preaching how the defaced image is made new in Christ.
blocks.es_reference: 4. El hombre es amado y redimible — su esperanza (Juan 3:16). Y aquí gira todo el arco. El Dios que grabó la imagen y la vio caer no se apartó de la ruina — “de tal manera amó Dios al mundo.” Pero este es el punto que se deja para que tú lo desarrolles en el Día 4, así que no diremos más de él aquí que esto, y te entregamos el gozo de predicar cómo la imagen desfigurada es hecha nueva en Cristo.

blocks.en: Day 4 — Developing the Points (E-A-I), then Your Turn
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — Desarrollando los puntos (E-A-I), luego su turno

blocks.en: Point 1 (the image of God, Genesis 1:26–27) developed in full:
blocks.es_reference: El Punto 1 (la imagen de Dios, Génesis 1:26–27) desarrollado por completo:

blocks.en: Explanation of the text. Alone among the creatures, man is made “in the image of God.” This is what sets a human being apart from the animals: the capacity to know God, to reason, to choose, to love, to create, and to be held responsible.
blocks.es_reference: Explicación del texto. Único entre las criaturas, el hombre es hecho “a imagen de Dios.” Esto es lo que distingue al ser humano de los animales: la capacidad de conocer a Dios, de razonar, de elegir, de amar, de crear, y de ser tenido por responsable.

blocks.en: Application of the text. So every person has dignity that no failure can cancel and no oppressor can revoke. The hearer who feels worthless is told a truth older than his shame: you bear the image of the living God. This is also why we treat the poor, the unborn, the elderly, and the enemy as sacred.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación del texto. Así que cada persona tiene una dignidad que ningún fracaso puede cancelar y ningún opresor puede revocar. Al oyente que se siente un don nadie se le dice una verdad más antigua que su vergüenza: llevas la imagen del Dios vivo. Por eso también tratamos como sagrados al pobre, al no nacido, al anciano y al enemigo.

blocks.en: Illustration. A coin bears the image of the king; however battered and dirty, it never loses its worth, because the image stamped on it is the king’s. So with the soul that bears God’s image.
blocks.es_reference: Ilustración. Una moneda lleva la imagen del rey; por golpeada y sucia que esté, nunca pierde su valor, porque la imagen grabada en ella es la del rey. Así con el alma que lleva la imagen de Dios.

blocks.en: I do, we do, you do. Point 2 (man has fallen, Rom. 3:23) we work together: Explanation — “all have sinned” puts every hearer in the same verdict, no exceptions. Application — the comparison game (“at least I’m better than him”) collapses; the standard is God’s glory, and all fall short. Illustration — (you supply it: a picture of falling short of a mark, not merely being bad. Reach for your own.) Then Point 4 (man is loved and redeemable, John 3:16) is yours: How does the image defaced become the image restored in Christ? How do you preach worth without flattery and hope without cheapness? Write your three paragraphs and the sermon is built.
blocks.es_reference: Yo lo hago, lo hacemos juntos, tú lo haces. El Punto 2 (el hombre ha caído, Ro. 3:23) lo trabajamos juntos: Explicación — “todos pecaron” pone a cada oyente bajo el mismo veredicto, sin excepciones. Aplicación — el juego de la comparación (“al menos soy mejor que aquel”) se derrumba; la norma es la gloria de Dios, y todos quedan cortos. Ilustración — (tú la aportas: una imagen de quedar corto de un blanco, no solo de ser malo. Busca la tuya.) Luego el Punto 4 (el hombre es amado y redimible, Juan 3:16) es tuyo: ¿Cómo la imagen desfigurada llega a ser la imagen restaurada en Cristo? ¿Cómo predicas el valor sin adulación y la esperanza sin abaratarla? Escribe tus tres párrafos y el sermón queda construido.

blocks.en: 💡 The defaced masterpiece: a great painting, smoke-darkened and torn, is still a masterpiece and worth restoring at any cost — the image defaced by sin, not destroyed (for Point 3 or 4).
blocks.es_reference: 💡 La obra maestra desfigurada: una gran pintura, ennegrecida por el humo y rasgada, sigue siendo una obra maestra y vale la pena restaurarla a cualquier costo — la imagen desfigurada por el pecado, no destruida (para el Punto 3 o 4).

blocks.en: 💡 The Filthy Rag (Isaiah 64:6): From the first man we inherited a sinful nature, and it runs so deep that even what look like our noblest motives are corrupt at the core. As the Bible says, “we are all like an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are like filthy rags” (Isaiah 64:6). Picture a clean rag. First the baby spits up and you wipe its chin. Then the toilet needs cleaning, so you use the rag for that. By now it is good for little — but then the dog has an accident on the floor, and you wipe that up too. Now the rag is untouchable. No one would pick it up; all you can do is throw it in the garbage. Now hear the verse again: your best efforts — your finest good works, offered to a holy God to earn your acceptance — are that rag. This is how deep the fall goes: not only our worst but our best is defiled. And it is why man cannot save himself, and why only Christ can make the unclean clean. (For Point 2 or 3.)
blocks.es_reference: 💡 El Trapo Inmundo (Isaías 64:6): Del primer hombre heredamos una naturaleza pecaminosa, y es tan profunda que aun lo que parecen nuestros motivos más nobles está corrompido en lo más hondo. Como dice la Biblia, “todos nosotros somos como cosa inmunda, y todas nuestras justicias como trapo de inmundicia” (Isaías 64:6). Imagine un trapo limpio. Primero el bebé vomita y usted le limpia la barbilla. Luego hay que limpiar el inodoro, y usa el trapo para eso. Ya sirve para poco — pero entonces el perro tiene un accidente en el piso, y también lo limpia. Ahora el trapo es intocable. Nadie lo recogería; lo único que puede hacer es echarlo a la basura. Ahora oiga el versículo otra vez: sus mejores esfuerzos — sus mejores buenas obras, ofrecidas a un Dios santo para ganar su aceptación — son ese trapo. Así de profunda es la caída: no solo lo peor de nosotros, sino lo mejor, está contaminado. Y por eso el hombre no puede salvarse a sí mismo, y solo Cristo puede limpiar lo inmundo. (Para el Punto 2 o 3.)

blocks.en: Day 5 — Craft Notes and Summary
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — Notas de oficio y resumen

blocks.en: Two cautions. Hold both halves of the paradox. Preach only man’s glory and you flatter him into never seeking a Savior; preach only his ruin and you crush him into despair. The gospel needs both: great enough to be worth saving, lost enough to need it. Always end at hope. The doctrine of man is not good news by itself — it is the bad news that makes the good news good. So the arc must reach Christ, who is both the true image (Col. 1:15) and the Savior of the fallen.
blocks.es_reference: Dos advertencias. Sostén las dos mitades de la paradoja. Predica solo la gloria del hombre y lo adulas hasta que nunca busque un Salvador; predica solo su ruina y lo aplastas en la desesperación. El evangelio necesita ambas: lo bastante grande para valer la pena salvarlo, lo bastante perdido para necesitarlo. Termina siempre en la esperanza. La doctrina del hombre no es buena nueva por sí sola — es la mala nueva que hace buena a la buena nueva. Así que el arco debe alcanzar a Cristo, que es a la vez la verdadera imagen (Col. 1:15) y el Salvador de los caídos.

blocks.en: Unit 5 has run the method on the doctrine of man: a lean backbone (image, fall, depravity, worth), the subject and keyword truths, four points each on a text, one point developed in full, one worked together, and one left to the preacher, and an arc from glory through ruin to hope. Unit 6 turns to the life and work of Christ.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 5 ha corrido el método sobre la doctrina del hombre: un fundamento breve (imagen, caída, depravación, valor), el tema y la palabra clave verdades, cuatro puntos cada uno sobre un texto, un punto desarrollado por completo, uno trabajado juntos, y uno dejado al predicador, y un arco de la gloria por la ruina a la esperanza. La Unidad 6 pasa a la vida y obra de Cristo.

blocks.en: "For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." — Romans 3:23 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios." — Romanos 3:23 (RVG)

mc.stem: The paradox the preacher must hold whole about man is that he is:
options: Crowned with glory yet fallen into ruin
mc.why: Man is at once God’s image-bearer and a sinner; the preacher must keep both halves.

mc.stem: The image of God in man (Genesis 1:26–27) is the ground of:
mc.why: The image of God is the ground of all human dignity — the reason every person matters.

mc.stem: Romans 3:23 teaches that:
options: All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory
mc.why: “All have sinned” places every hearer under the same verdict.

mc.stem: Depravity means:
options: We are as bad as we could possibly be
Sin touches no part of us
Sin reaches every part of us, so we cannot save ourselves
mc.why: Depravity means no part is untouched by sin, not that we are as bad as possible.

mc.stem: The image of God after the fall is:
mc.why: The fall defaced the image but did not erase it; man still bears it.

mc.stem: The preacher’s aim in preaching man is to:
options: Tell the truth that prepares for grace
mc.why: Neither flattery nor crushing, but the truth that readies the hearer for grace.

mc.stem: The order of the worked sermon’s points is:
mc.why: Glory → ruin → need → hope lifts, humbles, empties, then points to Christ.

mc.stem: Ephesians 2 anchors which point?
mc.why: Ephesians 2:1, 8–9 anchors man’s need — dead in sin, saved by grace, not works.

mc.stem: The coin illustration teaches that the image:
options: Keeps its worth however battered, because it is the king’s image
mc.why: A battered coin keeps its worth because the king’s image is stamped on it — so the soul.

mc.stem: John 3:16 anchors which point?
options: Man is loved and redeemable (his hope)
mc.why: John 3:16 anchors man’s hope — loved by God and redeemable.

mc.stem: To preach only man’s glory and never his ruin will:
options: Flatter him into never seeking a Savior
mc.why: Glory without ruin flatters; the hearer never sees his need of a Savior.

mc.stem: To preach only man’s ruin and never his worth or hope will:
mc.why: Ruin without hope crushes; the gospel needs both halves.

mc.stem: The doctrine of man is best described as:
options: The bad news that makes the good news good
mc.why: Man’s ruin is the bad news that makes grace shine; it must reach the gospel.

mc.stem: Why does the doctrine of man treat the poor, unborn, elderly, and enemy as sacred?
options: Because each bears the image of God
mc.why: The image of God grounds the dignity of every person, including the weak and the enemy.

mc.stem: In the worked sermon, the subject is ___ and the keyword is ___.
mc.why: Subject: man; keyword: truths (about man).

mc.stem: The defaced-masterpiece illustration teaches that man is:
options: Damaged but worth restoring at any cost
mc.why: Like a smoke-darkened masterpiece, the image is defaced, not destroyed, and worth redeeming.

mc.stem: “All have sinned” collapses which common human strategy?
options: The comparison game (“at least I’m better than him”)
mc.why: If all fall short of God’s glory, comparing ourselves to others proves nothing.

mc.stem: Colossians 1:15 calls Christ:
options: The image of the invisible God
mc.why: Christ is the true image of God, the One in whom our defaced image is restored.

mc.stem: “You are greater than you think and worse than you fear” means man needs to hear:
options: Both his dignity and his sin
mc.why: The hearer must hear both halves so that only Christ answers both.

mc.stem: The arc of a sermon on man should end at:
mc.why: The doctrine ends at hope: Christ, the true image and the Savior of the fallen.

sa.prompt: State the paradox the preacher must keep whole in preaching the doctrine of man, and the preacher’s aim.
sa.model: The preacher must keep whole the paradox that man is at once crowned with glory and fallen into ruin: he is made in the image of God, and yet he is a sinner. The aim is not to flatter the hearer by preaching only his greatness, nor to crush him by preaching only his sin, but to tell him the truth that prepares him for grace. The hearer must hear both halves, that he is greater than he thinks and worse than he fears, so that he sees only Christ answers both. Hold one half alone and the gospel is lost; hold both and the hearer is readied for grace.

sa.prompt: Lay out the homiletical move for a sermon on man: subject, interrogative, keyword, and how the points stay biblical.
sa.model: The subject is man. The interrogative asked of it is, what is the truth about man? The keyword that answers is truths, a plural noun from which the outline grows. The keyword yields four points, that man is made in God’s image, that he has fallen into sin, that he cannot save himself, and that he is loved and redeemable. The points stay biblical because each one rests on its own text rather than on the preacher’s opinion. The preacher arranged the truths, which makes the sermon topical and deductive, yet it remains the teaching of Scripture because every point is anchored to a passage.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that man is made in the image of God, and why it matters.
sa.model: To be made in the image of God means that man, alone among the creatures, was created with the capacity to know God, to reason, to choose, to love, to create, and to be held responsible. This is what sets a human being apart from the animals. It matters because the image is the ground of all human dignity and worth: every person, however weak or sinful, has a value that no failure can cancel and no oppressor can revoke, simply because the image of God is stamped on them. This is the reason we treat the poor, the unborn, the elderly, and even the enemy as sacred.

sa.prompt: What does depravity mean, and what does it NOT mean?
sa.model: Depravity means that sin reaches every part of us, so that no part of our nature is left untouched, and therefore we cannot save ourselves. What it does not mean is that we are as bad as we could possibly be, or that every person commits every sin. The point is extent, not intensity: sin has spread into mind, will, and affections alike, defacing the image throughout. This is why salvation must come from outside us as a gift, for a being whose every faculty is touched by sin cannot lift himself out of it by his own power.

sa.prompt: Develop “Man is made in God’s image” (Genesis 1:26–27) as a sermon point using Explanation, Application, and Illustration.
sa.model: The Explanation is that, alone among the creatures, man is made in the image of God, with the capacity to know God, reason, choose, love, and be responsible; this sets the human being apart from the animals. The Application is that every person therefore has a dignity that no failure can cancel and no oppressor can revoke, so the hearer who feels worthless is told a truth older than his shame, and we treat the weak and even the enemy as sacred. The Illustration is the coin that bears the image of the king: however battered and dirty it becomes, it never loses its worth, because the image stamped on it is the king’s, and so it is with the soul that bears the image of God.

sa.prompt: Name the four truths in the worked sermon, in order, with the text under each.
sa.model: The worked sermon preaches four truths in order, each on its own text. First, man is made in God’s image, his glory, on Genesis 1:26–27. Second, man has fallen into sin, his ruin, on Romans 3:23. Third, man cannot save himself, his need, on Ephesians 2:1 and 8–9. Fourth, man is loved and redeemable, his hope, on John 3:16. The order moves from glory to ruin to need to hope, lifting the hearer, humbling him, emptying him, and then pointing him to Christ.

sa.prompt: Why is the ORDER of the points (glory, ruin, need, hope) the power of the sermon?
sa.model: The order is the power of the sermon because it takes the hearer on a journey that prepares him for the gospel. First the truth of the image lifts him, showing his glory and worth. Then the truth of the fall humbles him, showing his ruin. Then his inability to save himself empties him of self-reliance, showing his need. And finally the love of God in Christ gives him hope. Reverse or scramble the order and the effect is lost; in this sequence the hearer is raised, brought low, stripped of self-trust, and then pointed to Christ, which is an arc that bends naturally toward the invitation.

sa.prompt: Why must a sermon on man hold both his glory and his ruin, and never just one?
sa.model: A sermon on man must hold both his glory and his ruin because each half without the other does harm. To preach only his glory is to flatter the hearer so that he never sees his need and never seeks a Savior. To preach only his ruin is to crush him into despair, with no reason to hope. The gospel needs both: man is great enough to be worth saving, because he bears God’s image, and lost enough to need saving, because he has fallen. Only when the hearer holds both does grace make sense, for grace is God redeeming a glorious creature from a real ruin.

sa.prompt: How does the doctrine of man drive the hearer toward the gospel and toward Christ?
sa.model: The doctrine of man is not good news by itself; it is the bad news that makes the good news good. By showing the hearer both his lost glory and his real ruin, it creates the need that only the gospel can meet, so the sermon must always reach Christ rather than ending in despair. Christ is the answer to both halves of the paradox: He is the true image of the invisible God, in whom our defaced image is restored, and He is the Savior of the fallen, who loved us and gave Himself for us. So the doctrine drives the hearer from what he is to the One who can both restore his image and redeem his ruin.

sa.prompt: Summarize how Unit 5 turns the doctrine of man into a sermon, from backbone to arc.
sa.model: Unit 5 runs the method on the doctrine of man. It begins with a lean backbone: man is made in God’s image, he has fallen into sin, depravity touches every part so he cannot save himself, yet he keeps worth as God’s image-bearer. Then it makes the homiletical move, taking the subject man, asking what is true about him, and using the keyword truths to yield four points, each anchored to its own text and ordered glory, ruin, need, hope. One point, the image of God, is developed by Explanation, Application, and Illustration, with one worked together and one left to the preacher. Finally the sermon bends from glory through ruin to hope in Christ, never resting in flattery or despair. Backbone, method, worked example, and arc to hope: the same template as every doctrine unit.
